title: Problem solving: model, pattern, eliminate, guess and check
summary: Four ways to solve a problem: list every case in order, find the pattern, cross out what can't be, and guess, check and improve.
guide: The Iranian Year 2 book teaches one {{term:problem-solving-strategy}} in each chapter. This studio puts four of them side by side, one per mission: make a model (list every case in order), look for a pattern, eliminate impossible cases, and guess and check. The problems come from those lessons.
Make a model: "to find every case in a problem, write them down in order so that you know none is missing." Your child writes the cases in a table; the "altogether" column works itself out.
Look for a pattern: your child sees the jumps between the numbers (+2, +3, +4) and carries the pattern on. The usual slip is to repeat the last jump.

Eliminate: every case is already written; your child crosses out the ones that break the rule. Guess and check: your child guesses a number, the table shows whether it is too small or too big, and the next guess gets better. The "why" question at the end of each mission is the look-back step.

model-pockets.title: Make a model: marbles in two pockets
model-pockets.prompt: Reza has 6 marbles and puts them in his 2 pockets. One pocket may stay empty. In how many ways can he do it? Write every case in order in the table: 0 marbles in the left pocket, then 1, then 2, …
model-pockets.hint: In every row the two pockets hold 6 marbles altogether. Put 0, 1, 2, … in the left pocket until you reach 6. If you run out of rows, tap "add a row".
model-pockets.success: Well done! 0 and 6, 1 and 5, 2 and 4, 3 and 3, 4 and 2, 5 and 1, 6 and 0: Reza can do it in 7 ways.
model-pockets.why: Why does writing the cases in order (0, 1, 2, …) help you not miss any?
model-pockets.model: Because the left pocket gets one more marble each time and the right pocket one fewer. I start at 0 and stop at 6, so no number is missed and no case is written twice. 0 and 6 count too, because a pocket can be empty.

feedback.known-missing: You missed a fact you need. The number of marbles and the number of pockets both matter.
feedback.known-extra: Does the colour of the marbles change the number of ways?
feedback.asked-wrong: The problem already tells us that: 2 pockets. What don't we know?
feedback.table-empty: Fill the table: in each row, write how many marbles are in the right pocket.
feedback.list-wrong: In one row the two pockets don't hold 6 marbles altogether. Look at the "altogether" column.
feedback.list-repeat: You have written one case twice. Each case only once.
feedback.list-missing: Some cases are still missing. Fill the left pocket in order 0, 1, 2, … up to 6. If you run out of rows, tap "add a row".
feedback.no-empty: Don't forget the cases with an empty pocket: 0 and 6, and 6 and 0.
feedback.one-empty: Count the rows again. 0 and 6 is different from 6 and 0: the empty pocket has changed.
feedback.too-big: Count the rows of the table; each row is one way.
feedback.too-small: Count the rows of the table; each row is one way.
feedback.empty: Type your answer in the gap.

pattern-triangles.title: Look for a pattern: triangles of dots
pattern-triangles.prompt: We arrange dots in triangles. Shape 1 has 1 dot, shape 2 has 3 dots, shape 3 has 6 dots and shape 4 has 10 dots. If the shapes carry on in the same way, how many dots will shape 6 have?
pattern-triangles.hint: Look at the jumps in the table: +2, +3, +4. Each jump is one more than the last. What is the next jump?
pattern-triangles.success: Well done! The jumps are +5 and +6: 10 + 5 = 15 and 15 + 6 = 21. Shape 6 has 21 dots.
pattern-triangles.why: Why does each jump get one bigger? Think about the shapes.
pattern-triangles.model: Each shape adds a new row under the last one, and the new row has one more dot than the bottom row before. Shape 5 gets a row of 5 and shape 6 a row of 6. So shape 6 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21.

feedback.known-missing: You missed a fact you need. The first shapes and "in the same way" both matter.
feedback.known-extra: Does the colour of the dots change how many there are?
feedback.asked-wrong: The problem already tells us shape 4: 10 dots. What don't we know?
feedback.table-empty: Write the number of dots for shapes 5 and 6 in the table.
feedback.table-pattern: Look at the jumps: +2, +3, +4. They get one bigger each time; they don't stay the same.
feedback.same-hop: The jumps don't stay the same: +2, +3, +4, so the next one is +5, not +4 again.
feedback.figure-5: 15 dots is shape 5. Shape 6 has one more jump.
feedback.too-big: Look at the dots column in the table for shape 6.
feedback.too-small: Look at the dots column in the table for shape 6.
feedback.empty: Type your answer in the gap.

eliminate-cards.title: Eliminate: the cards 7, 0 and 9
eliminate-cards.prompt: There are 3 cards with 7, 0 and 9 on them. Using all three cards, how many three-digit numbers can we make? Every order of the cards is written below. Cross out the ones that are not three-digit numbers.
eliminate-cards.hint: If 0 comes first, like 079, the number is just 79: a two-digit number.
eliminate-cards.success: Well done! 079 and 097 are not three-digit numbers. That leaves 4: 709, 790, 907 and 970.
eliminate-cards.why: The cards 2, 3 and 5 make six three-digit numbers. Why do 7, 0 and 9 make fewer?
eliminate-cards.model: Because 0 can't be the hundreds digit. If 0 comes first there are no hundreds and the number has only two digits. So the two orders that start with 0 are crossed out: 6 − 2 = 4.

feedback.known-missing: You missed a fact you need: the cards, and that we use all three to make a three-digit number.
feedback.known-extra: Does the colour of the cards change the numbers?
feedback.asked-wrong: The problem already tells us the digits. What does it ask?
feedback.crossed-answer: You crossed out a real three-digit number. Tap it again to bring it back.
feedback.too-many-left: A number that isn't three-digit is still there. Which numbers start with 0?
feedback.zero-first: Not every order is a three-digit number. Don't count the ones you crossed out.
feedback.too-big: Count only the numbers that are not crossed out.
feedback.too-small: Count only the numbers that are not crossed out.
feedback.empty: Type your answer in the gap.

guess-legs.title: Guess and check: heads and legs
guess-legs.prompt: A farm has some sheep and some hens. Altogether they have 10 heads and 28 legs. How many sheep are there? Guess the number of sheep and try it.
guess-legs.hint: A sheep has 4 legs and a hen has 2. If there are fewer than 28 legs, guess more sheep; if there are more, guess fewer.
guess-legs.success: Well done! 4 sheep and 6 hens: 4 × 4 + 6 × 2 = 16 + 12 = 28 legs.
guess-legs.why: After your first guess, how did you know whether the next guess should be bigger or smaller?
guess-legs.model: If we swap one hen for one sheep, there are still 10 heads but 2 more legs. So when there were too few legs I guessed more sheep, and when there were too many, fewer. Each guess brought me closer.

feedback.known-missing: You missed a fact you need. The number of heads and the number of legs both matter.
feedback.known-extra: Does the distance to the village change the number of legs?
feedback.asked-wrong: The problem already tells us that: 10 heads. What don't we know?
feedback.no-guess: Guess a number of sheep and tap "Try it".
feedback.not-found: You haven't reached 28 legs yet. Too few legs: guess more sheep. Too many: guess fewer.
feedback.hens: 6 is the number of hens. The question asks for the sheep.
feedback.half-legs: 28 ÷ 4 = 7 would mean they are all sheep! But there are 10 heads, and the rest are hens.
feedback.too-big: In the table, find the row with exactly 28 legs.
feedback.too-small: In the table, find the row with exactly 28 legs.
feedback.empty: Type your answer in the gap.
